topics.title: Setup, Virtual Environments and pip
topics.summary: Install Python, create an isolated virtual environment and install packages with pip.
topics.description:
Python is an interpreted, general-purpose language known for readable syntax. Before writing real projects you need three things: the interpreter, a **virtual environment** and a package manager (**pip**).

### Running Python
- `python --version` checks the install (use `python3` on macOS/Linux).
- `python` opens the REPL, an interactive prompt for quick experiments.
- `python app.py` runs a script file.

### Why virtual environments?
Different projects need different versions of libraries. If you install everything globally, versions clash. A virtual environment (`venv`) is a private folder with its own Python and its own packages, so each project stays isolated.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate         # Windows
pip install requests
pip freeze > requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt
deactivate
```

### pip basics
`pip install name`, `pip install name==2.1.0`, `pip uninstall name`, `pip list`, `pip show name`, and `pip install --upgrade name`. A `requirements.txt` file lists the exact packages so someone else can recreate your environment. Newer projects often use `pyproject.toml` with tools such as Poetry or uv, but the idea is the same: declare dependencies, lock them, keep them isolated.

Always run `python -m pip ...` if you are unsure which Python a bare `pip` belongs to; it guarantees pip matches the interpreter.
keyPoints: Create one virtual environment per project with python -m venv .venv
Activate it before running pip so packages go into the project, not the system
pip freeze > requirements.txt records exact versions
python -m pip is safer than bare pip
Never commit the .venv folder; commit requirements.txt instead
pitfalls: Installing packages globally and hitting version conflicts
Forgetting to activate the venv, then wondering why an import fails

examples.title: Typical project setup
examples.code:
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows (use source .venv/bin/activate on Linux/macOS)
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install requests beautifulsoup4
pip freeze > requirements.txt
python main.py
examples.explanation: The full life cycle: create, activate, install, record and run.

interview.a: It isolates a project's dependencies so different projects can use different library versions without conflict.
It lists the exact packages and versions a project needs, so anyone can recreate the environment with pip install -r requirements.txt.

topics.title: Variables, Types and Input/Output
topics.summary: Names bound to objects, Python's core built-in types, type conversion and print/input.
topics.description:
In Python a variable is a **name that points to an object**. You do not declare a type; the object carries its type, and the same name can later point to a different type (dynamic typing). Python is still **strongly typed**: it will not silently add `"5" + 5`.

### Core built-in types
| Type | Example | Mutable? |
|---|---|---|
| `int` | `42` | no |
| `float` | `3.14` | no |
| `bool` | `True` | no |
| `str` | `"hi"` | no |
| `NoneType` | `None` | no |
| `list` | `[1, 2]` | yes |
| `tuple` | `(1, 2)` | no |
| `dict` | `{"a": 1}` | yes |
| `set` | `{1, 2}` | yes |

### Conversion and checking
Use `int("5")`, `float("2.5")`, `str(10)`, `bool(0)`. `type(x)` shows the type and `isinstance(x, int)` is the preferred check.

### Input and output
`print()` writes to the console; `sep` and `end` control separators. `input()` reads a line of text as a **string**, so convert it when you need a number.

```python
age = int(input("Age: "))
print("Next year:", age + 1)
```

### Naming
Use `snake_case` for variables and functions, `UPPER_CASE` for constants and `PascalCase` for classes. Names cannot start with a digit or use keywords like `class` or `for`.

Falsy values are `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `set()`, `None` and `False`; everything else is truthy.
keyPoints: Variables are names bound to objects; types belong to objects
Python is dynamically but strongly typed
int, float, bool, str are immutable; list, dict, set are mutable
input() always returns a string; convert it explicitly
Use isinstance() for type checks
pitfalls: Forgetting that input() returns str, so "2" + "3" gives "23"
Using a mutable default or alias without realising two names share one object

examples.title: Types and conversion
examples.code:
x = 10
y = 3.5
name = "Asha"
flag = True
nothing = None

print(type(x), type(y), type(name), type(flag), type(nothing))
print(int("42") + 1)
print(float("2.5") * 2)
print(str(99) + " is text")
print(bool(0), bool("hi"), bool([]))
print(isinstance(x, int))
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, round(0.1 + 0.2, 2) == 0.3)

a = [1, 2]
b = a          # same object, two names
b.append(3)
print(a, a is b)
examples.explanation: Shows types, conversion, falsy values and aliasing.

examples.title: print options
examples.code:
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")
print("no newline", end=" | ")
print("next")
x, y = 5, 10
x, y = y, x      # swap
print(x, y)

interview.q: Is Python statically or dynamically typed?
interview.a: Dynamically typed (types are checked at runtime) and strongly typed (no implicit unsafe conversions). Optional type hints add static checking via tools.

interview.q: What is the difference between == and is?
interview.a: == compares values; is compares identity, i.e. whether two names refer to the same object.
None, False, zero of any numeric type, and empty containers or strings.

topics.title: Operators
topics.summary: Arithmetic, comparison, logical, membership, identity and assignment operators.
topics.description:
Operators combine values into expressions.

### Arithmetic
`+ - * /` as usual. `/` always returns a float, `//` is floor division, `%` is the remainder and `**` is power.

### Comparison and chaining
`== != < > <= >=` return booleans. Python allows chains like `1 < x < 10`, which is read as `1 < x and x < 10`.

### Logical
`and`, `or`, `not`. They **short-circuit** and return one of the operands, not strictly `True`/`False`: `"" or "default"` gives `"default"`. This is a common idiom for fallback values.

### Membership and identity
- `in` / `not in` test membership in strings, lists, sets, dicts (keys).
- `is` / `is not` test whether two names point to the same object. Use `x is None`, never `x == None`.

### Assignment
`+=`, `-=`, `*=` etc. update in place. The walrus operator `:=` assigns inside an expression (Python 3.8+).

### Bitwise
`& | ^ ~ << >>` work on integers at the bit level, useful for flags and masks.

### Precedence (high to low)
`**`, unary `-`, `* / // %`, `+ -`, comparisons, `not`, `and`, `or`. When in doubt, use parentheses; they cost nothing and make intent clear.
keyPoints: / gives float, // floors, % is remainder, ** is power
Comparison operators can be chained: 1 < x < 10
and/or short-circuit and return an operand
Use "is None" for None checks
in tests membership; for dicts it checks keys
pitfalls: Using == None instead of is None
Expecting // to truncate toward zero: -7 // 2 is -4
Using is to compare numbers or strings

examples.title: Operators in action
examples.code:
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2, 2 ** 10)
print(-7 // 2, -7 % 2)
x = 5
print(1 < x < 10)
print("" or "default")
print(0 and 100, 3 and 100)
print("a" in "cat", 3 not in [1, 2])
n = 10
n += 5
print(n)
if (m := len("hello")) > 3:
    print("long word", m)
print(5 & 3, 5 | 3, 5 ^ 3, 1 << 4)

interview.q: What does // do with negative numbers?
interview.a: It floors the result toward negative infinity, so -7 // 2 is -4.
The first truthy operand, or the last operand if none is truthy. It does not always return a boolean.

topics.title: Strings and f-strings
topics.summary: Immutable text sequences, slicing, common methods and f-string formatting.
topics.description:
A `str` is an **immutable sequence of Unicode characters**. You can index and slice it, but you cannot change a character in place; every "modification" builds a new string.

### Creating
Single, double or triple quotes. Triple quotes allow multi-line text. Prefix `r` makes a raw string (backslashes kept, handy for regex and Windows paths).

### Common methods
`upper()`, `lower()`, `title()`, `strip()`, `split()`, `join()`, `replace()`, `find()`, `startswith()`, `endswith()`, `isdigit()`, `count()`.

### f-strings
The modern way to format. Put `f` before the quote and expressions inside `{}`:

```python
name, price = "Pen", 12.5
print(f"{name}: Rs {price:.2f}")
```

Format specs: `:.2f` (2 decimals), `:>10` (right-align width 10), `:,` (thousands separator), `:05d` (zero-pad), `:%` (percent). `f"{value=}"` prints the expression and its value, which is great for debugging.

### Joining and splitting
`",".join(["a", "b"])` is much faster than repeated `+` in a loop. `"a b c".split()` splits on whitespace.

### Encoding
Strings are Unicode; `.encode("utf-8")` gives `bytes`, and `.decode()` goes back. Always specify the encoding when reading or writing files.
keyPoints: Strings are immutable; methods return new strings
f"{x:.2f}" is the preferred formatting style
Use "sep".join(list) instead of += in loops
Slicing works on strings: s[::-1] reverses
Raw strings r"..." keep backslashes literally
pitfalls: Building big strings with += in a loop
Forgetting that split() with no argument also removes empty parts

examples.title: Methods and formatting
examples.code:
s = "  Hello, Python  "
print(s.strip().upper())
print(s.strip().split(", "))
print("-".join(["a", "b", "c"]))
print("python"[::-1])
print("banana".count("a"), "banana".find("n"), "banana".replace("a", "o"))

name, score, total = "Ravi", 87.456, 1234567
print(f"{name} scored {score:.1f}")
print(f"Total: {total:,}")
print(f"[{name:>8}] [{name:<8}] [{name:^8}]")
print(f"{score=}")
print(f"{7:03d}")
examples.explanation: Output shows common string methods and format specs.

interview.a: No. They are immutable; operations such as replace() or upper() return new strings.

interview.q: Why is join() better than += in a loop?
interview.a: Each += creates a new string and copies everything, which is O(n^2) overall. join() builds the result once.

topics.title: Conditionals and Loops
topics.summary: Branch with if/elif/else and repeat with for and while, including break, continue and else.
topics.description:
Python uses **indentation** (normally 4 spaces) to define blocks; there are no braces.

### Conditionals
```python
if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 75:
    grade = "B"
else:
    grade = "C"
```
A one-line form is the conditional expression: `label = "adult" if age >= 18 else "minor"`.

Python 3.10 added `match`/`case` for structural pattern matching, a cleaner replacement for long `elif` chains.

### for loops
`for` iterates over any iterable: lists, strings, dicts, ranges, files. Use `range(start, stop, step)` for numbers, `enumerate()` for index plus value and `zip()` to walk several sequences together.

### while loops
`while condition:` repeats until the condition is false. Always make sure something changes inside the loop.

### Loop control
- `break` leaves the loop.
- `continue` jumps to the next iteration.
- `else` on a loop runs only if the loop finished without `break`, handy for search patterns.
- `pass` is a do-nothing placeholder.

### Pythonic tips
Prefer `for item in items` over indexing with `range(len(items))`. Use `enumerate` when you need the index, and `zip` rather than manual index juggling.
keyPoints: Indentation defines blocks
range(), enumerate() and zip() make loops clean
break exits, continue skips, loop-else runs when no break happened
match/case gives pattern matching (3.10+)
Truthiness lets you write if items: instead of if len(items) > 0:
pitfalls: Infinite while loops because the condition never changes
Modifying a list while iterating over it

examples.title: for, while, else
examples.code:
for i, fruit in enumerate(["apple", "kiwi", "fig"], start=1):
    print(i, fruit)

for a, b in zip([1, 2, 3], "xyz"):
    print(a, b)

n = 5
while n > 0:
    n -= 2
print("n =", n)

for x in [4, 6, 8]:
    if x % 2 == 1:
        print("found odd")
        break
else:
    print("no odd numbers")

command = "stop"
match command:
    case "go":
        print("going")
    case "stop" | "halt":
        print("stopping")
    case _:
        print("unknown")

interview.q: When does the else clause of a for loop run?
interview.a: When the loop completes normally without hitting break.
